extracted.intended_audience: California state agency rulemakers, regulated parties, advocates, and members of the public interested in participating in California regular rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to conduct and participate in California's APA regular rulemaking process, including required documents, public participation rules, change-notice procedures, comment handling, OAL review, and effective-date rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public involvement in preliminary rulemaking activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, the rulemaking agency has discretion whether to include the public during preliminary rulemaking activities; however, if a proposed rulemaking action involves complex proposals or a large number of proposals that cannot easily be reviewed during the comment period, the agency shall involve parties who would be subject to the proposed regulations. This requirement is not subject to OAL or judicial review. (Government Code section 11346.45.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary rulemaking is the research/gathering stage; public involvement is discretionary except where complexity or volume makes early involvement necessary to allow meaningful review during the formal comment period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express Terms (required document)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text of the proposed regulation will clearly identify any changes to the California Code of Regulations; proposed additions appear as underlined and proposed deletions appear in strike-through format. The Authority and Reference citations that follow the text of each regulation section identify the statutes on which the section is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express terms are one of at least four documents required to initiate formal rulemaking; they must show exact proposed text changes and include Authority/Reference citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of Proposed Action (required document)
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of proposed action contains a variety of information about the nature of the proposed regulatory changes including various findings, determinations, statutory authority and the law(s) being implemented. The notice of proposed action also contains procedural information, such as deadlines for submitting comments, scheduling of hearings (if any), and where copies of the express terms, initial statement of reasons, and any other supporting information can be obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice must be published in the California Regulatory Notice Register and mailed to persons who requested notice; it triggers start of APA rulemaking and specifies contact, deadlines, and access to supporting documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial Statement of Reasons (required document)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial statement of reasons is a document that explains the reasons why the agency is making the proposed regulatory changes, including an explanation of the problem being addressed, the purpose of and necessity for, and benefits of the proposed changes. It identifies the factual material upon which the agency relies and includes required determinations, findings and analyses including either the economic impact assessment (for non-major regulations) or standardized regulatory impact analysis (for 'major regulations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must list materials relied upon; contains determinative analyses that later constrain reliance on newly added materials without a 15-day notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and Fiscal Impact Statement (Form STD. 399) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Form STD. 399 is a Department of Finance form an agency is required to complete and have signed by the rulemaking agency's highest ranking official or that official's delegate. The Form STD. 399 includes information on the estimated economic (private) and fiscal (governmental) monetary impacts of the proposed regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules governing the Form STD. 399 are in the State Administrative Manual, sections 6600 through 6615; signature by agency head or delegate is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the formal rulemaking process begins (publication/posting/mail and one-year deadline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To initiate formal rulemaking, an agency publishes a notice of proposed action in the California Regulatory Notice Register, mails the notice to those who requested notice, and posts the notice, express terms, and initial statement of reasons on the agency's website. Once published in the Register, the APA rulemaking process is officially started and the agency has one year to complete the rulemaking and submit the completed rulemaking file to OAL. (Government Code section 11346.5.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication triggers statutory timelines and filing obligations; posting on the agency website and mailing are required alongside Register publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum written public comment period and submission instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires a minimum 45-day period for the public to comment to the agency in writing on the proposed regulation. The notice of proposed action specifies the rulemaking agency name, contact person and address where the comments must be directed and the date the written comment period closes. Members of the public should not submit written comments on regular rulemaking actions to OAL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the contact and deadline specified in the notice; do not send comments to OAL for regular rulemaking actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public hearing procedures and requester rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency has the option to hold a public hearing. If an agency does not schedule a public hearing, any interested person can submit a written request for a hearing at least 15 days prior to the close of the written public comment period; if timely requested, the agency must hold a public hearing. If a public hearing is held, it must be scheduled for a date at least 45 days after the notice was published. At the public hearing, both written and oral comments must be accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requesting a hearing timely obligates the agency to hold it; hearings accept both oral and written comments and must respect the 45-day scheduling minimum following publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of changes to proposed text — nonsubstantial changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsubstantial changes do not alter the regulatory effect of the proposed provisions; therefore, no further notice is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a change only clarifies or corrects without changing effect, agency need not provide additional comment opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of changes to proposed text — substantial and sufficiently related
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial changes alter the meaning of the regulatory provisions and, if sufficiently related (i.e., reasonably foreseeable based on the notice of proposed action), must be made available for public comment for at least 15 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before adopting such a change the agency must mail a notice of opportunity to comment on proposed changes along with the text of the proposed changes to each person who submitted written comments, testified at the hearing, or asked to receive notices of proposed modification, and post the notice on its website. No public hearing is required. The public may comment only on the proposed modifications in writing. The agency must consider any comments received during the 15-day period. An agency may conduct more than one 15-day opportunity to comment before adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of changes to proposed text — substantial and not sufficiently related
rubrics_metrics.description: If a change is substantial but not sufficiently related to the original proposal (i.e., not reasonably foreseeable based on the notice of proposed action), the agency must publish another 45-day notice in the California Regulatory Notice Register similar to the original notice of proposed action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These kinds of changes are uncommon but require restarting the full 45-day notice-and-comment cycle via a new Register publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding documents to the rulemaking record after initial statement of reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: A rulemaking agency must specifically identify any material the agency is relying upon for the proposed rulemaking in the initial statement of reasons. If during the proceeding an agency decides to rely on material not identified in the initial statement of reasons, the agency must make the document available for comment for 15 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 15-day availability/notice is similar to the 15-day notice for substantial, sufficiently related text changes and limits reliance on unseen materials without opportunity to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency duty to summarize and respond to public comments (Final Statement of Reasons)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rulemaking agency must summarize and respond to timely comments that are directed at the proposal or at the procedures followed by the agency during the rulemaking action. For each comment, the agency must include either an explanation of how the proposed action has been changed to accommodate the comment or state the reasons for rejecting the comment. In summarizing and responding to public comments, the agency must demonstrate that it understood and considered the comment. The summary and response to comments is included as part of the rulemaking file in a document called a Final Statement of Reasons. (Government Code section 11346.9.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses must show consideration and explain acceptance or rejection; the Final Statement of Reasons is part of the official rulemaking record.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAL review timing and possible outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: A rulemaking agency must transmit a rulemaking action to OAL for review within one year from the date the notice was published in the California Regulatory Notice Register. Once submitted, OAL has 30 working days to conduct a review of the rulemaking record to ensure the agency satisfied the requirements of the APA and OAL's regulations. OAL will then either approve the rulemaking action and file the proposed regulation with the Secretary of State or disapprove the rulemaking action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL review is time-limited (30 working days) and results in approval and filing with the Secretary of State or disapproval; the agency must meet the one-year transmission deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: When an approved regulation becomes effective (quarterly effective-date schedule and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, regulations become effective on one of four quarterly dates based on when the final regulations are filed with the Secretary of State: January 1 (if filed between Sept. 1 and Nov. 30); April 1 (if filed between Dec. 1 and Feb. 29); July 1 (if filed between Mar. 1 and May 31); and October 1 (if filed between June 1 and Aug. 31).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective dates may vary if a different effective date is provided in statute or other law, if the adopting agency requests a later effective date, or if the agency demonstrates good cause for an earlier effective date.
